name: Washington

notes: Food for home consumption, candy and gum included, is exempt; soft drinks, bottled water (since August 1, 2017) and dietary supplements are taxed at the full rate, which is not counted here.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer and wine are taxed at the full rate on top of their excise taxes. Spirits bought in stores pay no sales tax; they carry the 20.5% spirits sales tax and $3.7708 a liter instead, which are not counted here: they fall on only spirits, and no official figure gives spirits' share of alcohol bought in stores (the 2022 Economic Census doesn't split liquor stores' sales by kind); drinks served, spirits included, pay the ordinary state and local sales tax, counted for drinks served (bars and restaurants pay a 13.7% spirits tax and $2.4408 a liter when they buy spirits, a cost in the drink's price, not a tax on it, and not counted).

Cigarettes, other tobacco, nicotine and vapor products are taxed at the full rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: $3.025 a pack of cigarettes, 95% of the price on other tobacco products and, since January 1, 2026, on all nicotine products, nicotine vapor included (a legal challenge is pending), and 27 cents a milliliter on nicotine-free vapor liquid (9 cents above 5 mL).
Household supplies: diapers are taxed; an exemption starts January 1, 2029 (ESSB 6346 of 2026), as long as the 2026 income tax it came with is not struck down in court.

Personal care products: menstrual products are exempt (since July 1, 2020), which is not taken out here. Soap, shampoo, toothpaste, mouthwash, deodorant, sunscreen and over-the-counter drugs are taxed until January 1, 2029, when ESSB 6346 of 2026 exempts them on the same condition as diapers.
Barber and beauty services: haircuts and other hair and beauty services are not taxed; tanning, tattooing and steam baths are, which is not counted here.
Laundry and dry cleaning services are taxed; self-service (coin-operated) laundry is not.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and taxed by the gallon instead: 56.5 cents for gasoline and 59.5 cents for diesel since July 1, 2026 (up 1.1 cents), left out here.
Repair labor is a retail sale and taxed.
Washington has no sales tax holiday; clothing is taxed at the full rate.
No local restaurant or food and beverage tax applies: King County's ended October 1, 2011, and since 2018 state law bars new local taxes on groceries, drinks included (RCW 82.84.040).

The 2029 exemptions for diapers, hygiene products and over-the-counter drugs come with the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and lapse if a court strikes that tax down. Initiative 645, which would have repealed the income tax but not the exemptions (Attorney General's explanatory statement), failed on November 3, 2026, 830,106 for and 1,152,229 against (Secretary of State, unofficial count of November 4).
Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus local lodging taxes (in Seattle, 15.7% in all), which are not counted here (DOR lodging rates, fourth quarter 2026).
gaps: Washington rates are by DOR location code (each city, unincorporated county area, transit area and tribal area has its own); the place rate is the most common code's rate.

4 cities lie in more than one county with a different rate in each county part; in each census tract such a city's rate is that of its part in the tract's county, counted for the share of the tract's store jobs located in the city.

The rate file lists the current rates of Walla Walla County and 18 other jurisdictions (cities, transit or special districts) only through a date before April 1, 2027, with nothing after them (a renewal may not be filed yet); the current rates are used.

Local sales tax votes on November 3, 2026, by the counties' unofficial counts (November 4; counties certify November 24): new or higher taxes approved in Seattle, SeaTac, Milton, Shelton, Liberty Lake, Moses Lake and Pierce Transit's service area, each from April 1, 2027 at the earliest, and renewals in Mount Vernon and Chehalis; these are noted on those pages. The Department of Revenue's notices of January 1, 2027 increases (posted November 2026) name King, Snohomish, Kitsap, Spokane, Grays Harbor and Thurston counties and Auburn, Bellevue, Bonney Lake, Centralia, Concrete, Elma, Granite Falls, Issaquah, Kelso, Kenmore, Longview, Marysville, Monroe, Orting, Pasco, Port Angeles, Raymond, Ruston, SeaTac, Shoreline, Snoqualmie, Spokane, Stanwood, Tenino, Twisp, Union Gap, Vancouver, West Richland and Woodinville; some are noted on their pages, and all count from the Department's January rate workbook, not yet posted; the rates here are those in effect from October 1, 2026. No county's full list of November measures could be found for Adams, Columbia, Douglas, Ferry, Garfield, Grays Harbor, Jefferson, Lincoln, Pacific, Wahkiakum, Walla Walla, Whitman and Yakima counties.

Outside cities, the local rate depends on which transit districts cover an address, and sales tax is charged where purchases are made, so each census tract takes the average rate where its stores are, in cities or not (store jobs, and jobs at restaurants, bars and hotels for restaurant meals and drinks served: LEHD LODES 2024 by census block; residents, 2020 census, for a tract with no such jobs), from DOR's location-code map; county figures show the rate that covers the most residents outside cities.

King County's own 0.1% for its transportation benefit district comes on top from the same date.

The current rate, which includes it, is used here.

tiers.label: Washington distressed area
tiers.what: Counties whose three-year average unemployment rate (2023 to 2025) is at least 20% above the state's, 5.4% or more (RCW 43.168.020). Agencies use the list to decide eligibility for grants, incentives and programs that support economic recovery and job growth.
tiers.none: Not a distressed area (three-year unemployment under 5.4%)

tiers.label: Washington rural county
tiers.publisher: Washington State Office of Financial Management
tiers.what: Counties with fewer than 100 people per square mile, or smaller than 225 square miles, or with no city over 45,000 people (RCW 82.14.370). Many state laws and rules use this definition to target rural counties for assistance.
tiers.none: Not a rural county under RCW 82.14.370

programs: Business improvement areas are mapped for Seattle (10), downtown Tacoma and Spokane (Downtown and East Sprague). Seattle's Tourism Improvement Area, an assessment on hotel stays, is left out. Everett's downtown improvement district isn't mapped: the city's open-data layer draws it as set in 2017 (Ordinance 3582-17, last updated May 2023), and the city expanded it in December 2025, as reported by the Daily Herald. The Everett Station business improvement area has no map.

Washington's six Community Empowerment Zones (Duwamish, White Center, Spokane, Tacoma, Yakima and Bremerton) aren't drawn yet: the Department of Revenue publishes them as map images and in its tax rate lookup, not as a boundary layer. Businesses there can still claim the state's business and occupation tax credit for new jobs (RCW 82.62), which the Department of Revenue lists among its current incentives; only the sales and use tax deferral that once applied in the zones (RCW 82.60) has ended, on July 1, 2020.

Local tax increment areas (chapter 39.114 RCW, since 2021) are mapped for Spokane (three, and the University District revitalization area), Pasco (five) and Douglas County (East Wenatchee); others, among them Bellevue's Grand Connection area (in effect June 1, 2026), aren't mapped (no official map found). The Main Street program's communities (Department of Archaeology and Historic Preservation) and the 25 certified creative districts (ArtsWA) have no published boundaries and aren't shown.

warn.text: Port Townsend draws many visitors, but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of Port Townsend's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

SeaTac holds Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and 53 lodging places (1.6 per 1,000 residents), and the city counts a daily visitor population more than six times its residents (City of SeaTac, 2026 ballot statement), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Travelers' spending is part of SeaTac's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Walla Walla draws many visitors (wine country), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of Walla Walla's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Snoqualmie draws many visitors (Snoqualmie Falls and the Snoqualmie Casino nearby), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
